newsitem.title: USA: U.S. criticizes China for jailing monk.
newsitem.headline: U.S. criticizes China for jailing monk.

text.p: The United States on Thursday criticized China for imprisoning a senior Tibetan monk convicted of separatist activities and leaking state secrets.

A court in Tibet last month sentenced Chadrel Rinpoche to six years in prison for colluding in 1995 with the Dalai Lama, Tibet's exiled spiritual leader, to choose a 6-year-old Tibetan boy, Gedhun Choekyi Nyima, as the new Panchen Lama.

The move enraged atheist China, which named another 6-year-old Tibetan, Gyaincain Norbu, instead. Many Tibetans see the Beijing-anointed boy as a false pretender. The whereabouts of Gedhun Choekyi Nyima are not known.

"The United States is deeply disturbed by this decision," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said. "We urge China to ensure full exercise of religious freedom as set forth in its own constitution."
Burns noted that Rinpoche's trial was held in secret without due process safeguards. "This, of course, does not meet international standards -- any notion of international standards," he said.
He urged Beijing to release all those imprisoned for expressing divergent religious or political beliefs.
"And we urge China to preserve Tibet's unique cultural, linguistic and religious heritage," he added.
Burns said the United States regarded the mechanism for formally recognizing or identifying a reincarnated Lama as a religious matter and, therefore, would not take a specific position on the issue.

"But we clearly feel that since the Dalai Lama has recognized a reincarnated Lama -- a young boy and his family -- that that boy should be returned and allowed to practice his religion freely," he said.
"That has not happened, so we do have very deep-seated concerns about what is happening in Tibet to people who simply want to practice their religion," Burns told reporters.

He also urged Tibetan Buddhists and the Chinese government to work out the steps to recognizing a reincarnated Lama, adding that the United States had "not identified an individual who we would recognize."
Chinese troops marched into Tibet in 1951 and suppressed a rebellion in the region in 1959 that forced the Dalai Lama and thousands of followers to flee into exile in India.
The Dalai Lama won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1989 for his non-violent campaign for more autonomy for his homeland.
